claims.method: AGGREGATION: median of three lens positions (structural-proxy 13, reference-class 11.5, decomposition 13.8). The R3 upward correction from 12 is UPHELD and is now supported by two independent linage traditions that both land at 15-16 percent of national newspaper linage in 1914-16. || ROUTE 1, the 52-city linage band, WEIGHT 0.45. Input: HSUS T 485-486, classified 18-21 percent of newspaper linage in every year 1928-1941. PROXY-POPULATION GAP: a metropolitan panel eleven years after the window against a 1914 universe of 2,580 dailies among 22,754 publications. ADJUSTMENTS: universe correction, direction down, size -3.8pp; period correction for the 1920s growth of help-wanted, used-automobile and suburban-real-estate classified, direction down, size small and poorly evidenced. || ROUTE 2, the Chicago Tribune 1916 observation, WEIGHT 0.30. Input: Field 1916, advertising volume 'about equally divided between classified and display'. PROXY-POPULATION GAP: the country's leading want-ad daily is the extreme upper tail of the distribution whose mean is wanted. ADJUSTMENT: scale by a top-paper-to-average ratio calibrated on 1928, where the 52-city average was 19.2 percent while leading want-ad papers ran near 50 percent (ratio 2.0-2.5x); direction down, size -60 percent from the raw figure. || ROUTE 3, linage-to-receipts rate conversion, WEIGHT 0.25. Input: the NAA 1950 revenue identity (classified $377m of $2,070m = 18.2 percent of newspaper revenue) at a 22-27 percent linage share, which solves the unmeasured rate ratio r at 0.60-0.79; Rogers 1918's two-cents-per-word card. PROXY-POPULATION GAP: every measured series is LINAGE and the target is RECEIPTS, and r is the hinge no source states. ADJUSTMENT: apply r = 0.70 (band 0.55-0.90) to a 15-19 percent linage share, giving 11-14 percent of receipts. || The literature's claim that pre-WWI classified was materially below the 1928 level is asserted and unmeasured, and the one in-window observation runs the other way. INTERVAL widened to [8, 22] on the panel spread. NOTE THE BASIS: this is a share of newspaper RECEIPTS. claims.statement: Direct-response buyers - mail-order houses, patent-medicine makers and every advertiser working a keyed reply - spent about $192 million in 1914, roughly 16 percent of the benchmark total. The anchor is now Printers' Ink of 4 May 1911, which tabulates direct mail at $100 million, farm and mail-order at $75 million, sampling at $18 million, distributing at $6 million and house organs at $7 million, in window and contemporaneously.
claims.unit: USD millions (current), 1914 benchmark
claims.method: Buyer-side dollar reading of the era's direct-response pool: 16.0 percent of the $1,200m 1914 benchmark. ANCHOR UPGRADED, under the rule that where a real source exists it wins. Printers' Ink of 4 May 1911 p. 79 states the component channels in window and contemporaneously - direct mail $100m, farm and mail-order $75m, demonstration and sampling $18m, distributing $6m, house organs $7m - and its twelve lines sum exactly to its stated $616m total. The 1926 Britannica's $300m for 1920, which the record previously carried as the primary anchor, is retained only as a corroborating route: deflating it for the price level (CPI x1.99 over 1914-1920) and for real growth (+15 to +25 percent) gives about $126m for 1914, within 12 percent of the PI-derived $113m direct-mail line. || ROUTES AND WEIGHTS are those of e1-scale-014. D1, the PI 1911 direct lines grown x1.131 to 1914, WEIGHT 0.35, with direct mail split 65 percent direct response / 20 percent business-to-business / 15 percent local retail (proxy-population gap: direct mail was not one money type; the 50-80 percent range on that first share is the largest lever here). D2, mail-order sales x expense ratio, WEIGHT 0.30, US mail-order trade sales $325-365m at an 8-14 percent all-in advertising ratio validated from catalogue production arithmetic rather than assumed. D3, the Britannica back-cast, WEIGHT 0.15, adjusted for the price level and for real growth, direction down on both. D4, the direct-mail share-of-total path across 1911, 1920, 1935 and 1950, WEIGHT 0.20, which pins Coen-basis direct mail at 10-12 percent of the 1914 total and is the only route constraining how the measured base maps onto the broad benchmark. CEILING: Adams 1905 caps ALL patent-medicine advertising of every kind at roughly $25-33m. || The pool grades C for two reasons that are not resolvable: no source in the era uses the term 'direct response', so assigning these channels to it is interpretation; and the $75m farm-and-mail-order line does not say how much is periodical space rather than mail-order houses' own outlay - a $0-85m swing, larger than the gap between this pool's central and national brand's.

claims.statement: National brand advertising was about 22 percent of total US advertising outlay at the 1914 benchmark, roughly $264 million of $1,200 million. It is joint-largest with local retail, and no surviving evidence separates the two. This supersedes the 16 percent the record carried before the money-type re-research.
claims.unit: percent of total US advertising outlay
claims.method: SOURCED BY: no source. No compiler in or out of the window states national advertising as a share of total US advertising for any year 1840s-1917. The pool rests on three sourced inputs that each cover only part of it (ANPA national newspaper dollars for 1915 via Borden via Galbi, third-hand; Census of Manufactures 1914 other-periodicals receipts $71.586m, grade A but receipts rather than outlay and never split by class of advertiser; the Printers' Ink 4 May 1911 channel lines, grade B and contemporaneous but enumerating MEDIA rather than money types). Grade stays C because every route from those inputs to this pool is a construction. || AGGREGATION: plain median of three lens centrals (structural-proxy 36.1, reference-class 22, decomposition 17.0). No extremizing, per PROCESS.md: the three lenses share one evidence base, so they are not informationally independent and extremizing would push the aggregate outside the panel. Five independent routes survive after collapsing near-duplicates. || R1 ANPA newspaper national share, re-based from space to outlay, WEIGHT 0.25. Input: ANPA 1915 national $55m against local-including-classified $220m, i.e. 20.0 percent of newspaper money; Census 1914 newspaper receipts $184.047m x the documented 1.5187 Galbi wedge = $279.5m of newspaper outlay. PROXY-POPULATION GAP: ANPA measures newspaper SPACE at gross card rate in 1915, not total outlay in 1914. ADJUSTMENTS: deflate 1915 to 1914 at the Census newspaper-receipts growth rate of about 4.4 percent a year, direction down, size -5 percent; raise national's share of OUTLAY above its share of SPACE, because national money carried materially more preparation per dollar of space (plates and electrotypes cut once and shipped to hundreds of papers, agency art and copy), direction up, size +3pp. Result about 23 percent of newspaper outlay, about $64m. NEAR-DUPLICATES COLLAPSED: all three lenses ran this same ANPA pair; counted as ONE route. || R2 Census other-periodicals decomposition, WEIGHT 0.20. Input: 1914 other-periodicals advertising receipts $71.586m x 1.5187 = $108.7m of outlay. PROXY-POPULATION GAP: the Census class bundles consumer magazines with farm, trade, business, technical and religious papers, which are not one money type. ADJUSTMENT: strip business and technical papers (about 28 percent of the class) to the business-to-business residual as dealer- and engineer-directed money, and split farm papers (about 17 percent) between national brand and mail order; direction down, size -38 percent of the class, giving about $60-74m. This is the single largest correction to the superseded reading, which took the whole periodicals line at 70-100 percent national. || R3 Printers' Ink 1911 channel build grown to 1914, WEIGHT 0.25. Input: the twelve published channel lines, which sum exactly to the stated $616m, grown at the Census newspaper-receipts ratio x1.131, with a national fraction applied channel by channel. PROXY-POPULATION GAP: PI enumerates MEDIA, not money types, and publishes its newspaper line as one undivided 'retail and general' $250m. ADJUSTMENT: novelty (calendars, fans, matchbooks) was predominantly given away by local merchants and billposting carried heavy theatrical and circus money, so the out-of-home and promotion block is taken at 50-70 percent national; direction down, size -45 percent of the block, giving about $64m. || R4 buyer-count x appropriation Fermi build, WEIGHT 0.15. Input: six advertiser tiers, from the Crowell top-75 national magazine advertisers ($13.7m of magazine spend, 1919) down to 30,000 regional and sectional brands and 25,000 trade-paper-only industrial advertisers. Touches none of R1-R3's inputs. PROXY-POPULATION GAP: the Crowell series begins in 1919, two years past the era close, and covers magazines only. ADJUSTMENT: deflate on the Census other-periodicals receipts ratio (71.6/154.8 = 0.463) and gross up to all media at a 40 percent magazine weight; both analyst-set, neither sourced, and the deflator risks overcorrecting because periodical receipts nearly doubled 1914-19 on wartime prices. || R5 reference-class continuity from the first measured partition, WEIGHT 0.15. Input: Coen 1935 national $890m of $1,720m = 51.7 percent, with non-newspaper media 77.4 percent national; ANPA's 20.0 percent newspaper national share in 1915 against Coen's 19.4 percent in 1935, flat across the era boundary. PROXY-POPULATION GAP: 1935 postdates the era by 21 years and Coen's two-way taxonomy has no direct-response category, so mail-order and patent-medicine money sits inside 'national'. ADJUSTMENTS: strip radio, which did not exist in 1914 and was about 6.6 percent of the 1935 total and overwhelmingly national, direction down; reclassify the mail-order and patent-medicine block out of national into direct response, direction down, size -12 to -18pp. || NOT ROUTES. Rogers 1919 p. 319 (national about 30 percent of a mid-size daily's linage, about 50 percent of its net income) is a coherence check, reconciled rather than averaged by reading the 50 percent as a MARGIN statement. Cherington 1913 and the N. W. Ayer patent-medicine revenue shares are documentary pull, not measurement. The below-the-line uplift that lifts the structural-proxy lens from 15.6 to 36.1 is a DENOMINATOR TREATMENT rather than a route to this pool, which is why the plain median and not a weighted mean is the correct aggregator here. || INTERVAL: min lower bound to max upper bound across the three lenses. Its width is denominator-treatment disagreement, not measurement disagreement: on the channel-enumerated basis the lenses agree on this pool to within about one point.

claims.statement: Local retail advertising, excluding classified, was about 22 percent of total US advertising outlay at the 1914 benchmark, roughly $264 million. It ties with national brand as the joint-largest money type, and every route that raises one mechanically lowers the other.
claims.unit: percent of total US advertising outlay
claims.method: SOURCED BY: no source for the pool. The only in-window dollar figure is ANPA's newspaper local line, whose own column header says it INCLUDES classified ($220m in 1915), and no compiler has ever separated the two. Sourced inputs: ANPA via Borden via Galbi (third-hand); the Harvard Bureau of Business Research's measured advertising-to-net-sales ratios (grade A/B, in window, directly measured, but the retail-sales denominator they multiply is constructed). Grade stays C. || AGGREGATION: plain median of three lens centrals (structural-proxy 36.4, reference-class 22, decomposition 22.0). No extremizing; shared evidence base. Three routes survive, one of them only half-independent. || L1 ANPA local line net of classified, plus local out-of-home, WEIGHT 0.40. Input: ANPA local-including-classified $220m for 1915; total newspaper outlay 1914 $279.5m (Census receipts x 1.5187); local shares of the PI 1911 out-of-home and promotion lines grown to 1914 (novelty about 50 percent, billposting about 35, outdoor 45-50, streetcar 22-40, theatre programmes about 70, distributing 50-75, plus 14-15 percent of the direct-mail line as merchants' circulars). PROXY-POPULATION GAP: the ANPA line is 1915 and bundles classified, and classified must be subtracted on a RECEIPTS basis rather than a linage basis. ADJUSTMENTS: deflate 1915 to 1914, direction down, size -8 percent; remove classified at about 12 percent of newspaper receipts, -$22m. Basis check performed: ANPA's implied total newspaper money for 1914 is about $262m against the Census-derived $279.5m, 6 percent apart, so the ANPA basis needs no re-scaling. NEAR-DUPLICATES COLLAPSED: all three lenses ran this same ANPA line; ONE route. || L2 Harvard expense ratios x retail sales, WEIGHT 0.40. Touches no ANPA input and no Printers' Ink input - the only genuinely clean second route in the era. Input: Harvard's measured ratios by trade; US retail sales 1914 constructed at $15.8-17.5bn from nominal GDP $36,831m x a retail-to-GDP ratio of 0.43-0.47 taken from the 1929 Census of Distribution. THREE PROXY-POPULATION GAPS, each adjusted. (a) Trade mix: Harvard's spread across trades is an order of magnitude, so a single blended ratio is indefensible; trade-weighting food 28-30 percent at 0.15-0.2 percent, general merchandise 11-14 percent at 3.0 percent, apparel and shoes 10-13 percent at 2.0 percent, drug, furniture and hardware about 15 percent at 1.5-3.0 percent, automotive 7-10 percent at 0.8-1.2 percent, remainder at 0.5-1.0 percent gives 1.0-1.23 percent weighted, well below a naive blend. (b) Population: Harvard measures RETAIL STORES only, while the money type also holds local services - theatres and amusements, banks, hotels and restaurants, real-estate brokers, physicians, undertakers; direction up, size +15 to +30 percent. (c) Basis: the Harvard ratio is BOOKED advertising expense and already includes the store's own preparation, window trim and circulars, so it is comparable to the outlay basis and must NOT be scaled by the 1.5187 receipts wedge; applying the wedge here would double-count. KNOWN WEAKNESS CARRIED, NOT HIDDEN: Barger (NBER 1955), the correct retail-sales source, was located but not opened by any lens, and no in-window Harvard department-store bulletin exists, so importing a 1920s department-store ratio biases this route up. || L3 reference-class local-advertising-to-retail-sales ratio at 1935 and 1950, WEIGHT 0.20, HALF-INDEPENDENT. Input: Coen local 1935 $830m less about $90m classified = $740m against about $33bn of retail sales = 2.2 percent; Coen local 1950 $2,440m less $377m classified = $2,063m against about $145bn = 1.4 percent. PROXY-POPULATION GAP: 1935 is a depression year with a collapsed sales denominator, which inflates the ratio, so 1950 is the cleaner reading. ADJUSTMENT: band 1.3-1.7 percent applied to the same $17bn 1914 retail-sales figure L2 uses. DECLARED NOT INDEPENDENT: L3 shares L2's constructed denominator, so L2 and L3 are one-and-a-half routes, not two, and their agreement is partly mechanical. || THE KEY CROSS-CHECK: L1 and L2 share no input at all - one runs through ANPA newspaper dollars, the other through retailer profit and loss ratios on retail sales - and they land within 5-22 percent of each other in every lens that ran both. That is the strongest independent convergence in era 1 and it is what caps this pool. It also rejects a naive reference-class projection: carrying Coen's 1935 local share of 48.3 percent straight back would put local at about $580m, which requires a blended advertising-to-sales ratio above 2 percent that the Harvard grocery bulletin directly contradicts. || INTERVAL: min lower to max upper across the three lenses. The structural-proxy lens's 36.4 comes from the same below-the-line denominator treatment described under e1-scale-011, not from a different measurement of the money.

claims.statement: Classified advertising was about 2.2 percent of total US advertising outlay at the 1914 benchmark, about $26 million. It was the smallest of the four money types by a wide margin, and that is the one ordering this era can honestly assert.
claims.unit: percent of total US advertising outlay
claims.method: SOURCED BY: NO SOURCE FOUND, and this is a documented negative result rather than an unfinished search. No compiler published a classified dollar figure, a classified share or a classified linage series for any year 1840s-1917. Exhausted: the Census of Manufactures printing and publishing bulletins 1879-1919 (receipts enumerated but never split by class of advertising); HSUS T 485-491 and Millennial De516-522 (both start 1928, both sourced to Media Records Inc., trademark filed November 1928); Coen via Galbi (no classified category ever, no national/local partition before 1935); ANCAM (founded 1920); PIB (1945); SRDS (1919, and it publishes rates not spend); NAA (1950 onward); the Library of Congress inventory of historical marketing data (nothing pre-1919); and Printers' Ink 4 May 1911, which has NO classified line among its twelve channels. The best in-window evidence is firm-level and about LINAGE: Field 1916 on the Chicago Tribune. Grade C, and it cannot be raised by further search. || AGGREGATION: plain median of three lens centrals (structural-proxy 2.2, reference-class 2.2, decomposition 2.4) - the tightest agreement in the panel, reached from three different route mixes. Four routes survive after collapsing near-duplicates, plus one correction all three lenses made independently. || C1 Media Records 52-city linage band, back-projected and universe-adjusted, WEIGHT 0.30. Input: HSUS T 485-486 - classified was 18-21 percent of newspaper linage in 52 cities in EVERY year 1928-1941 (1928 19.2 percent, 1930 18.1, 1933 18.5, 1936 19.2, 1938 20.8, 1940 20.7), a band that held through a 44 percent collapse in total linage. TWO PROXY-POPULATION GAPS, both adjusted downward. (a) Period: the series starts eleven years after the window, and help-wanted, used-automobile and suburban-real-estate classified all expanded in the 1920s (motor registrations rose roughly tenfold 1915-29); direction down, size small and poorly evidenced, and partly offset by the band's stability through the Depression. (b) Universe: the 52-city panel is metropolitan, while the 1914 universe was 2,580 dailies among 22,754 publications and far more weekly-heavy. ADJUSTMENT: if metro papers carried about 60 percent of newspaper money at 19-25 percent classified and small papers ran 8-12 percent, the national average is about 15-19 percent of linage; direction down, size -3.8pp, LARGER than the period adjustment and pointing the same way. || C2 Chicago Tribune 1916 scaled by a calibrated top-paper-to-average ratio, WEIGHT 0.20. Input: Field 1916, about 50 percent of linage at the country's leading want-ad daily. PROXY-POPULATION GAP: the Tribune is the extreme upper tail of a distribution whose mean is the quantity wanted. ADJUSTMENT: calibrate the top-paper-to-average ratio on the one year where both exist in the same measurement tradition - the 52-city average was 19.2 percent in 1928 while leading want-ad papers ran near 50 percent, a ratio of 2.0-2.5x - then apply it in reverse to Field's 50 percent, then apply C1's small-paper universe adjustment; direction down, size -60 percent from the raw figure. Result about 16 percent of national linage in 1916, landing on C1 from a wholly different and IN-WINDOW source. That two independent traditions converge at 15-16 percent of linage is this pool's strongest result. || C3 linage-to-receipts rate conversion calibrated on the NAA 1950 revenue identity, WEIGHT 0.20. Input: NAA 1950 newspaper revenue - national $518m, retail $1,175m, classified $377m of $2,070m, so classified was 18.2 percent of newspaper REVENUE in 1950; Rogers 1918 prints a two-cents-per-word classified rate. PROXY-POPULATION GAP: the rate ratio r (classified revenue per agate line over display revenue per agate line) is the single unmeasured hinge and no source in or out of the window states it. ADJUSTMENT: solve revenue_share = L*r/(L*r + (1-L)) for r at the plausible 1950 classified linage share of 22-27 percent, which yields r = 0.60-0.79, far above the naive metropolitan rate-card comparison of 0.3-0.4, for two structural reasons - classified is set solid with no white space so every agate line is paid words, and classified carried no 15 percent agency commission and no contract discount. Use r = 0.70 (band 0.55-0.90). Applying it to a 15-19 percent linage share gives 11-14 percent of newspaper receipts. || C4 transaction-count Fermi, WEIGHT 0.20. Shares no input with any linage or revenue series - the only fully independent route here. Input: about 20.5m US households of which about 10m urban; urban households placing want ads, 30 percent of 10m at 2 orders = 6m; employers placing help-wanted against very high period labour turnover, 500,000 firms at 6 a year = 3m; landlords, rooming-house keepers and real-estate agents, 1m at 4 a year = 4m; lost-and-found, personals, business opportunity, livestock and agents-wanted 3m; about 16m orders at a blended $1.50. PROXY-POPULATION GAP: the two-cents-per-word rate is a metropolitan card, so small-town rates bias the average order value DOWN while a roughly 10 percent tail of standing dealer, agency and rooming-house contracts at about $8 biases it UP, the second being the larger term. Result 13.0 percent of newspaper receipts. || C5 newspaper-total reconciliation residual, WEIGHT 0.10, upper bound only. Forces newspaper outlay $279.5m less national about $64m less local-retail newspaper display (from the independent L2 build, $150-180m), bracketing classified at $36-66m of newspaper money on a space basis. || THE CORRECTION ALL THREE LENSES MADE INDEPENDENTLY, and the most consequential result of this pass: the documented 1.5187 Coen-to-Census wedge must NOT be applied to classified. That wedge is agency commission plus cost of preparation, and classified was the era's one channel with neither - no agency, no plates, no copy, no position charges, cash over a counter, with Rogers 1918 carrying 'Expenses, Classified' as its own sub-ledger. Classified outlay therefore equals classified receipts, so classified's share of OUTLAY sits BELOW its share of RECEIPTS (about 13 percent of receipts maps to about 8 percent of newspaper outlay), which REVERSES the direction of the adjustment the superseded reading applied. The corollary the chapter should carry: the wedge is ASYMMETRIC by money type - above 1.5187 for national brand (implied display-only wedge about 1.58), roughly 1.15-1.25 for local retail placed direct with the paper, and 1.00 for classified. Directory and telephone classified listings are carried at $3-4m (band $2-8m) as this pool's only non-newspaper component. || INTERVAL: min lower to max upper across the lenses. Its width is driven by two treatment levers, not by measurement: the rate ratio r (0.55-0.90) and the wedge treatment. The upper bound of 5.0 is what classified becomes if a future pass rejects the no-wedge argument and applies the full 1.5187 factor.

claims.statement: Direct-response money - catalogues, direct mail, and keyed print space bought by mail-order houses and patent-medicine makers - was about 16 percent of total US advertising outlay at the 1914 benchmark, roughly $192 million. It cannot be ranked against national brand or local retail.
claims.unit: percent of total US advertising outlay
claims.method: SOURCED BY: PARTIAL, and materially better sourced than the superseded record. Printers' Ink of 4 May 1911 p. 79 publishes the component channels IN WINDOW and CONTEMPORANEOUSLY - direct mail $100m, farm and mail-order $75m, demonstration and sampling $18m, distributing $6m, house organs $7m - and that sourced tabulation supersedes the 1926 Britannica back-cast as this pool's primary anchor. The POOL still grades C for two reasons recorded at source and not resolvable: no source in the era uses the term 'direct response', so assigning these channels to it is interpretation; and the $75m 'farm and mail-order' line does not say how much is space bought in farm and mail-order journals (a medium) versus advertising placed by mail-order houses (a money type) - a $0-85m swing. || AGGREGATION: plain median of three lens centrals (structural-proxy 16.0, reference-class 19, decomposition 14.0). No extremizing; shared evidence base. All three lenses moved this pool DOWN, for two named mechanical reasons rather than one judgment. Four routes survive after collapsing near-duplicates, plus one binding ceiling. || D1 Printers' Ink 1911 direct lines re-based to 1914, WEIGHT 0.35. Input: the five channels above, grown x1.131 to 1914 - direct mail $113m, farm and mail-order $85m, sampling $20m, distributing $7m, house organs $8m. PROXY-POPULATION GAP: direct mail in 1914 was not one money type; it carried consumer order-seeking mail, manufacturers' dealer and trade literature, and local merchants' house-to-house circulars. ADJUSTMENT: split 65 percent direct response, 20 percent business-to-business, 15 percent local retail, with the 50-80 percent range on that first share the single largest lever in this pool; house organs are predominantly dealer- and employee-directed, take 40 percent; sampling is largely national-brand trial generation rather than order-seeking, take 15-30 percent. || D2 mail-order sales x expense ratio, WEIGHT 0.30. Input: Sears about $101m of sales in 1914, Montgomery Ward about $45m; the two at 40-45 percent of the trade implies total US mail-order sales of $325-365m; the all-in advertising ratio for a mail-order house runs 8-14 percent of sales against store retail's about 1.1 percent, because the catalogue IS the store. PROXY-POPULATION GAP: no source states a mail-order advertising ratio, so it is validated rather than assumed - Sears's four-pound, 1,200-page big book at roughly $0.40-0.60 a copy over 15-20m mailed pieces a year gives $7.5-12m, i.e. 8-12 percent of sales, which reproduces the ratio from physical production arithmetic. ADJUSTMENT: apply 8-14 percent to $325-365m of trade sales. PARTIAL DEPENDENCE DECLARED: one lens's version of this route also leans on a Printers' Ink-derived residual, so only the sales-ratio half is clean; the clean half reproduces that residual ($48.3m against $48.0m) from a wholly different derivation, which is what resolves the farm-and-mail-order break toward mail-order houses' own outlay. || D3 Britannica 1920 back-cast, WEIGHT 0.15. Input: the 1926 Encyclopaedia Britannica's direct mail 'about $300,000,000' for 1920. PROXY-POPULATION GAP: six years past the era close, retrospective and tertiary. ADJUSTMENTS: deflate for the price level, CPI roughly doubled 1914-1920 (30.1 to 60.0, x1.99), direction down; deflate for real growth, +15 to +25 percent of real expansion over 1914-20 boosted by Liberty Loan and war-agency mail, direction down. $300m / (1.99 x 1.20) = about $126m for 1914, against D1's $113m, 12 percent apart. The value of running this route is not its estimate but its retirement: it shows the two anchors are mutually consistent and removes the record's reliance on the back-cast as primary. || D4 direct-mail share-of-total path across four observations, WEIGHT 0.20 - THE DISCRIMINATING ROUTE. Input: direct mail as a share of each compiler's own total - 16.2 percent in the PI 1911 table (100/616), 10.2-12.1 percent in 1920 (Coen $2,480m over HSUS $2,935m), 16.4 percent in 1935 (HSUS T 464 $282m over T 444 $1,690m), 14.1 percent in 1950 (Coen $803m of $5,700m). PROXY-POPULATION GAP: each share sits on its own compiler's denominator, and the pre-1919 denominator is not like-for-like with the post-1935 one. ADJUSTMENT: the observed path pins Coen-basis direct mail at 10-12 percent of the 1914 total, i.e. $120-144m, only 6-27 percent above the contemporaneous PI line, because the PI direct-mail and mail-order lines are ALREADY all-in production-plus-postage figures and barely scale when the basis broadens, while pure space money scales by roughly its own value again. This is the only route that constrains how the measured base maps onto the broad benchmark, and it rests on observed post-window readings rather than judgment: an even spread of the $503m basis gap would require a direct-mail line far above 12 percent of the total and CONTRADICTS the observed 1920 and 1935 readings. || THE BINDING CEILING (a constraint, not a route, WEIGHT 0). Adams, Collier's, 7 October 1905, put total US consumer spending on patent medicines at $75m. Grown to about $110m of retail by 1914, with manufacturers taking about 55 percent and spending about 40 percent of that on advertising, the ENTIRE patent-medicine category's advertising of every kind cannot exceed roughly $25-33m, of which only the keyed and mail-order portion is direct response. The superseded reading assigned $30-50m to patent-medicine KEYED PRESS ALONE. Caveat carried: Adams's $75m is a round number in a polemic, and at $200m of real retail spending the ceiling relaxes and this pool rises 2-3 points. || WHY THE POOL FELL. Two named mechanical causes, not a judgment call. (1) Double counting: the superseded method added mail-order and patent-medicine KEYED PRESS on top of a direct-mail base, but that keyed space is already inside the newspaper and periodical lines counted in the other pools; it also added premiums, samples and novelties wholesale, which the PI channel table places largely with national brand and local retail (novelty $30m was mostly local-merchant giveaway, sampling $18m mostly national-brand trial generation). Worth 4-5 points. (2) The patent-medicine ceiling above, worth 2-3 points. The basis correction is separate from and additional to both. || INTERVAL: min lower to max upper across the lenses.

claims.statement: The four money-type pools account for 62.2 percent of the 1914 benchmark, leaving 37.8 percent - about $454 million - unattributed. Roughly 5 to 9 points of that is a real fifth money type: business, trade and technical papers, legal, financial and government notices, and institutional and political money. The rest is the undocumented gap between a contemporaneous channel enumeration and a retrospective benchmark, and it is not a money type.
claims.unit: percent of total US advertising outlay
claims.method: RECONCILIATION IS FORCED AND EXACT. The four pool medians sum to 62.2 percent of the $1,200m observed total (national brand 22.0 + local retail 22.0 + classified 2.2 + direct response 16.0), leaving 37.8 percent = $454m unattributed; 22.0 + 22.0 + 2.2 + 16.0 + 37.8 = 100.0 exactly. The residual is reported as its own figure, not absorbed. Lens centrals: structural-proxy 9.3, reference-class 34.8, decomposition 44.7. || IT DECOMPOSES INTO TWO PARTS THAT MUST NOT BE CONFLATED. PART ONE, roughly 5-9 points ($60-112m): a GENUINE FIFTH MONEY TYPE the four-way taxonomy cannot hold - business, trade and technical paper advertising (the Census other-periodicals class is about 28 percent business and technical papers, dealer- and engineer-directed money), dealer-directed direct mail, house organs, legal, financial and government notices in newspapers, theatrical and circus billposting, and institutional, transportation and political advertising. Two lenses sized it independently at 9.3 and 5.2 percent, and it is corroborated forward: Coen's business-papers line was $76m of a $1,690m total in 1935, or 4.5 percent, with legal and financial notices a further 2-4 percent of newspaper linage. This part is real money with a real name and should be a labelled series in any chart. PART TWO, roughly 29-33 points ($350-400m): a DENOMINATOR ARTEFACT, the gap between a contemporaneous channel enumeration and a retrospective benchmark that nobody has ever decomposed. It is not a money type and must never be drawn as one. || THE GAP'S SIZE AND WHY IT EXISTS. Two anchors exist for 1914 and they are 1.72x apart. The MEASURED base is $697-725m: the twelve Printers' Ink channels, which sum exactly to their stated $616m, grown to 1914 at the Census newspaper-receipts ratio x1.131 = $697m, plus window display and directory listings. It is independently corroborated by Starch 1914 p. 7 ('nearly $700,000,000 are spent annually' on printed advertising), and its newspaper line reproduces the documented 1.5187 receipts-to-outlay wedge to within 1.1 percent (1.5356 against 1.5187). The RETROSPECTIVE benchmark is $1,200m. The $503m difference is 42 percent of the denominator, and the SAME PUBLISHING HOUSE's contemporaneous 1911 tabulation runs 38-46 percent below its own retrospective series for adjacent years, with no documented reconciliation anywhere. || TWO READINGS, BOTH CARRIED, NEITHER AVERAGED AWAY. READING A: the gap is genuine cost of preparation and non-media promotion, which the HSUS source note for series T 444-471 says is inside the basis - in which case it IS buyer money and belongs to the pools, allocated by below-the-line intensity (national brand about 1.4x space money, local retail about 0.7x, direct response about 0.5x because its lines are already all-in, classified about 0.0x), and the residual collapses to the fifth pool alone at 5-9 percent. That is the structural-proxy lens's position and the source of the interval's lower bound of 5. READING B: the gap is retrospective overstatement in the Printers' Ink / Coen lineage, in which case it stays unallocated at 43-55 percent. That is the decomposition lens's position and the source of the upper bound of 55. The consolidated central sits between them, closer to B, because the median rejected the full allocation that only one of three lenses performed. || THE GAP CANNOT BE SPREAD EVENLY, and this is a positive finding rather than a caveat. The measured-base lines are not on a common basis with each other: newspapers, periodicals and out-of-home are SPACE-ONLY (about $467m of the $697m), while direct mail, mail-order, novelty, sampling, distributing and house organs are ALL-IN production figures (about $230m). Broadening the denominator lifts the space pools by roughly their own value again and barely moves the all-in pools. The direct-mail share path is the check that confirms it: direct mail was 10-12 percent of the total-outlay basis in 1920 and 16.7 percent in 1935, so it cannot have been 25-30 percent in 1914, which an even spread would require. || INTERVAL: min lower to max upper across the lenses (structural-proxy [5,18], reference-class [22,45], decomposition [33,55]). No lens was discounted. The width is not sloppiness - it IS the finding. The three lenses agree on the evidence and disagree only on what the denominator contains, and no compiler has ever documented that.

claims.statement: World advertising expenditure in 1949 was on the order of $7.5 billion, of which the United States was roughly 70 percent. No contemporaneous world survey exists for this era.
claims.unit: US$ billions of estimated world advertising expenditure, 1949
claims.method: Two paths. (a) Bottom-up: US spend $5.21B at 1.9 percent of GDP; rest-of-world GDP in current dollars at 1949 official rates was roughly 1.5-2.5x US GDP of $267B, i.e. $400-670B, at an advertising intensity of 0.4-0.8 percent (war-damaged Europe and Japan, newsprint shortages, non-commercial state broadcasting), giving $1.6-5.4B outside the US and a world total of $6.8-10.6B. (b) Top-down share: the US ran roughly 60-65 percent of world advertising when the first systematic world surveys began in the late 1960s, and its share in 1949 must have been higher because commercial broadcasting was still almost exclusively an American institution; a 60-80 percent US share puts the world total at $6.5-8.7B. Both paths overlap in the $6.5-8.7B band; central set at $7.5B with a deliberately wide interval. The IAA/Starch INRA Hooper 'Survey of World Advertising Expenditures' does not begin until the 1960s.

claims.statement: For a corporation paying the wartime excess-profits tax, a dollar of deductible advertising cost roughly 20 cents after tax.
claims.unit: US$ after-tax cost to an excess-profits-tax-paying corporation of $1.00 of deductible advertising, 1943-45
claims.method: The Revenue Act of 1942 set a flat 90 percent excess-profits rate, but paired it with an overall ceiling limiting combined normal tax, surtax and excess-profits tax to 80 percent of surtax net income, and with a post-war refund credit of 10 percent of the excess-profits tax. Four cases: 90 percent with the credit ignored = 10 cents; 90 percent with the credit valued = 19 cents; at the 80 percent ceiling with the credit ignored = 20 cents; at the ceiling with the credit valued = 28 cents (the NBER marginal-rate methodology computes this case as R = .8 x .9 = .72). Most excess-profits payers sat at or near the ceiling, so the modal figure is 19-20 cents; central set at 20, interval spanning all four cases. Secondary accounts of the period ('the government might pay up to 80 percent') agree with the 20-cent figure.

claims.statement: Triangulated world advertising expenditure in 1975: roughly $54 billion, of which the United States was about 52%. No period source for a world total could be located, so this is a built estimate, not a found one.
claims.unit: billion USD of world advertising expenditure
claims.method: Two paths. (1) GDP-ratio path: World Bank world GDP 1975 = $6,048bn, US GDP = $1,685bn, so non-US GDP = $4,363bn. US advertising intensity was 1.66% of GDP; non-US intensity in 1975 was materially lower (developed Europe and Japan roughly 0.8-1.2%, the rest of the world well under 0.3%), giving a blended non-US rate of about 0.55% and non-US spend of $24bn; world = 27.9 + 24 = $52bn, US share 54%. (2) Bloc build-up path: OECD-ex-US GDP of roughly $2.7tn at ~0.9% gives $24bn, plus the rest of the world at roughly $1.7tn and ~0.3% gives $5bn; world = $57bn, US share 49%. Central is the midpoint of the two paths. Interval spans a blended non-US intensity of 0.33% to 0.97%.

The apparent three-route corroboration is one route wearing three hats, which is why the interval stays wide. || E1 Coen national/local geography residual, WEIGHT 0.60. claims.statement: US direct-response advertisers' measured media spend in 2000 was about $61.2B, 24.7 percent of the market: direct mail $44.6B, national directories $2.1B, performance-priced internet $0.7-1.4B and direct-response money bought inside general media $5-18.5B. claims.unit: USD billions (2000 US ad spend)
claims.method: SOURCED BY: PARTIAL, at component level only. Direct mail $44,591m is Coen's own published line (grade B) and is 73 percent of this pool's central. No source publishes this POOL on this denominator. Two compilers publish incompatible direct-response objects and BOTH are LARGER than the superseded construction: MAGNA's 'Direct' domain (grade A, free for 2000 via Statistical Abstract Table 1279) at $31,108m on a $177.5bn supplier-revenue universe, and DMA/WEFA (grade B) at $191.6bn on a $339.3bn universe that counts $73.2bn of telemarketing. Neither is commensurable with the Coen denominator, so neither wins outright; both constrain the interval and both raise the floor. Grade C. || AGGREGATION: plain median of three lens centrals (structural-proxy 22.62, reference-class 24.71, Fermi-decomposition 31.102). The spread is the widest in the era and is driven by two disclosed convention choices, not by conflicting evidence. ROUTE CONSOLIDATION APPLIED BEFORE ANY WEIGHTING. The panel presented about fourteen named routes across three lenses; they collapse to eight independent evidence bases, because routes sharing a common input are one route. The Coen national/local geography residual was offered seven times, MAGNA via Statistical Abstract T1279 six times, the 1997 Economic Census three times, DMA/WEFA three times with three different discount factors, the Knight Ridder 10-K three times, and the IAB format and pricing shares five times. || E1 Coen's own direct mail and Yellow Pages lines, WEIGHT 0.45. Direct mail alone is 18.02pp of the 24.71pp central. PROXY-POPULATION GAP: none for the medium, but a basis gap that is stated rather than adjusted - Coen books direct mail at full advertiser program cost while every other Coen medium is space only. || E2 MAGNA 'Direct' domain, WEIGHT 0.15. PROXY-POPULATION GAP: MAGNA's direct mail is carriage-only supplier revenue at $18,250m against Coen's $44,591m full advertiser outlay, a documented 2.44x. ADJUSTMENT: substitute Coen's direct-mail line into MAGNA's own classification and gross the denominator by the same amount, giving $57,449m / $203,841m = 28.2 percent - and MAGNA's Direct excludes direct-response TV, print and radio and telemarketing by its own construction, so 28.2 percent is a FLOOR from an independent compiler's own structure. Two lenses derived this separately. || E4 DMA/WEFA direct-marketing-by-medium, WEIGHT 0.20, CEILING-SETTING. PROXY-POPULATION GAP, and it is large: DMA measures response-CARRYING placements and includes traffic generation (drive-to-store with a call to action), not response-BOUGHT money; it counts telemarketing as advertising; its newspaper direct-response share of 37.3 percent ($18.4bn) almost exactly reproduces NAA's classified ($19.6bn), so it double-counts against the classified pool; and its direct-mail line matches Coen to $9m, proving it is NOT independent on the very medium it appears to corroborate. ADJUSTMENT: applied raw it yields $104.2bn of general-media direct response and a 48.9 percent pool, which all three lenses reject; the discounts applied ranged from a 3x medium-by-medium discount (to $18.5bn) through a roughly 75 percent discount (to $7.9bn) to a bottom-up rebuild (about $5.0bn). || E10 and E11, the ERA/infomercial direct-response-TV build and the PIB 1993 magazine mail-order category, WEIGHT 0.15 combined. These are the ONLY genuinely independent checks on the general-media direct-response quantity, and both land at the bottom of the range: ERA's $11bn of US direct-TV sales less $8.5bn of shopping-channel owned airtime that is outside measured advertising implies $3.5-5.3bn of direct-response television against DMA's $21.9bn, and PIB's magazine mail-order category was 9.8 percent of Coen magazines in 1993 against DMA's 56.6 percent. || E6 IAB/PwC pricing-model split, WEIGHT 0.05. PROXY-POPULATION GAP: IAB's denominator ($8,087-8,225m) exceeds Coen's internet line ($6,507m), so the share must be applied to Coen's line or money absent from the denominator is imported. ARITHMETIC DEFECT CORRECTED: the superseded method took 10 percent of IAB's $8,225m ($822m) against a denominator carrying $6,507m of internet; on the Coen line it is $651m, so the old method imported $172m. || E9 USPS Standard Mail (A) postage revenue, WEIGHT 0.0 on the central but named because it ADJUDICATES the basis: at roughly $15-16bn in FY2000 it puts Coen at 2.8-3.0x postage (postage plus production, creative and list rental, i.e. total advertiser outlay) and MAGNA at 1.15x (media-owner revenue plus a thin margin). Since a money-type split asks where ADVERTISER money goes, Coen's basis is the correct one for this partition. This route narrows the interval rather than widening it. || STATEMENT DEFECT CORRECTED: the superseded method said direct-response television and print insertions 'are not separable in the Coen series'. Not separable in COEN is true; not separable is false - DMA/WEFA published them by medium for 2000 (DR-television $21.9bn, DR-newspaper $18.4bn, DR-magazine $9.8bn, DR-radio $7.7bn). claims.statement: On the cross-era comparable rule, where ALL directory money sits in the same intent pool eras 6 and 7 use, US local-retail advertisers' measured media spend in 2000 was about $58.9B, 23.8 percent of the market. That is the era-native pool (e5-buyers-011, $70.1B) less the local Yellow Pages block, $11.1B, which this rule books as money bought for a counted reply rather than as local money. Under the era-native geographic rule local retail leads direct response, 28.32 to 24.71; under this unified-intent rule direct response leads local retail, 29.21 to 23.82. The flip is exact and this one block is its sole cause. Under BOTH rules the two intervals still overlap, so the pair stays unranked by interval and a chart must not sort these two bars. No 1994-2001 evidence decides which rule is right; both are carried.
claims.unit: USD billions (2000 US ad spend)
claims.method: TAXONOMY: unified-intent. This is the CROSS-ERA COMPARABLE view of era 5's local-retail pool, and it is a declared definitional seam, not a correction. The era-native claim (e5-scale-011 / e5-buyers-011) stands unchanged at 28.32 percent and is the view era 5 reports on its own terms. || THE BLOCK THAT MOVES: local Yellow Pages, $11,135m in 2000, which is 4.4995 percent of the observed $247,472m Coen total. The national directory leg, $2,093m, already sits in direct response under both rules, so only the local leg moves. Both legs are Coen's own published Yellow Pages line for 2000 ($13,228m) split by advertiser geography. || DERIVATION: this claim inherits the era-native pool's whole evidence base, three-lens panel and aggregation rule, and changes exactly one convention. Central = 28.32 - 4.4995 = 23.82 percent, $70,084m - $11,135m = $58,949m. Every other input is untouched: the Coen Total Local residual (E1, weight 0.60), the 1997 Economic Census local receipts check (E3, weight 0.15), the supply-side and demand-side shopper-and-weekly classified fringe builds (E7/E8, weight 0.10 combined, independent of each other and agreeing within 12 percent), the DMA/WEFA local share of general-media direct response (E4, weight 0.05) and MAGNA Local as a ceiling only (E2, weight 0.10, interval only). The containment check still holds and was not re-run because it does not touch directories: NAA retail $21,409m + NAA classified $19,608m = $41,017m sits inside Coen's local newspaper line of $41,821m with $804m to spare, verified for all eight years. || INTERVAL, and it NARROWS rather than shifting whole. Native ci80 [20.8, 33.0], 12.2pp wide. UPPER BOUND: 33.0 - 4.4995 = 28.50. The native ceiling was set by the reference-class and Fermi lenses, both of which carried the local directory block inside this pool, so removing the block lowers the ceiling by the whole block. LOWER BOUND: unchanged at 20.8. The reconciliation attributes 4.50pp of the native 7.52pp downside to the directory convention alone; under this rule that convention is settled by construction, so what is left below the central is the 3.02pp of measurement and construction dispersion the lenses actually disagree about, and 23.82 - 3.02 = 20.80. Net width 7.70pp against the native 12.2pp: a definitional question worth 4.50pp has been retired by rule, and the interval is narrower because of it, not because anything was measured. || NO EVIDENCE ADJUDICATES THE RULE, and this claim does not pretend otherwise. Nothing published in 1994-2001 records what a Yellow Pages buyer thought it was buying, so no source hunt can settle whether a plumber's directory listing is a local business buying advertising or an advertiser buying a counted reply. Both readings are defensible and the project carries both: the geographic rule as era 5's native view, this unified-intent rule as the cross-era comparable one. The choice is an editorial rule, not a finding. MAGNA, the only compiler in the era-5 window that partitions by money type at all, uses the unified rule: all directories sit inside its Direct domain with no geographic split. || GRADE: C, unchanged. No compiler published a local-RETAIL pool in this window on either rule; only a Local GEOGRAPHY containing classified and directory money. Re-cutting an unsourced pool on a different editorial rule cannot raise its grade. || WHAT DOES NOT MOVE: national brand (e5-scale-010 / e5-buyers-010, 38.34 percent) and classified (e5-scale-012 / e5-buyers-012, 8.85 percent) are identical under both rules, because no directory money sits in either pool under either rule. They keep their native IDs and are not restated here; the alt split therefore carries two pools, not four. The era residual (e5-scale-014, -0.22pp) is also unchanged, because the block is moved between two pools inside the same partition and the four pools still sum to 100.22 percent. || EX-DIRECT-MAIL RAIL: on the media-space-only basis, where Coen's $44,591m direct-mail line is replaced by MAGNA's $18,250m carriage-only figure and the 2000 total falls to about $221,131m, the same block is 5.04pp. The reconciled geographic shares on that rail (national brand 43.6, local retail 33.1, classified 9.9, direct response 13.4) become, on this rule, local retail about 28.1 and direct response about 18.4, with national brand and classified unchanged. That is the only like-for-like footing on which era 5 can be set beside era 7's ex-direct-mail rail, and it must be read on this rule, because era 7 uses this rule.

Either way 2001 was only the fifth annual decline in the Coen series since 1934 (1938, 1942, 1961, 1991, 2001); across the full 1919-2007 series there are eleven, the others clustered in 1921 and 1930-1933.

claims.statement: US advertising expenditure as a share of nominal GDP in 2000 - the peak of the post-1960 series, not of the whole record. Silk & Berndt, whose MCE and IRS series both begin in 1960, put the 2000 shares at 2.3% (MCE) and 2.4% (IRS); Galbi's rendering of Coen gives 2.5%. Galbi's series back to 1919 shows higher shares through the 1920s (2.8% in 1920, 3.0% in 1922, 2.8-2.9% in 1923-1929), and Silk & Berndt separately record advertising's share of National Income peaking above 4% in the 1920s. The share fell below 2% after 2000 and did not return.

claims.statement: US World Wide Web advertising revenue in 1995. No audited series exists: the IAB/PwC report begins with 1996 and the Coen series has no internet line before 1997, so this is a reconstruction from contemporaneous research-house estimates.

claims.statement: Worldwide major-media advertising expenditure in 2000, the era's global peak. Zenith Media's series put global adspend at $289B actual for 1998 with $320B and $339B projected for 1999 and 2000; WARC's series records a 3.1% global decline in 2001.
claims.unit: USD billions (worldwide major-media ad spend, Zenith basis: excludes direct mail and directories)
claims.method: No free, audited global series exists for this period; the recurring commercial series (Zenith, Magna, GroupM, WARC) are licensed. Zenith's published forecast of $339B for 2000 is taken as the upper anchor and discounted slightly because it was made ex ante and the year came in weaker than forecast in the second half; the WARC-recorded -3.1% global decline in 2001 implies a 2001 level near $325B on the same basis. CI spans $300-380B to cover the definitional question of whether direct mail and directories are inside the 'major media' total. The lower bound is NOT justifiable from the US Coen total, which is an all-media measure including direct mail and directories and is not comparable to Zenith's major-media basis (the comparable US major-media figure for 2000 is roughly $150B). The bound instead reflects the spread between Zenith's ex-ante $339B forecast and the weaker outturn implied by the WARC-recorded -3.1% global decline in 2001.

claims.statement: National-brand advertising was 38.3 percent of the $247.5B US measured advertising market in 2000, about $94.9B: audience-bought brand money in television, magazines, business papers, national newspaper display, national out-of-home and national miscellaneous, after removing the direct-response and classified money that sits inside Coen's National geography. All three lenses put it first at this anchor, but its interval overlaps local retail's and the pair is carried as unranked.
claims.unit: percent of total US ad spend
claims.method: SOURCED BY: no source. No compiler in 1994-2001 published a national-BRAND pool; they published a National GEOGRAPHY containing direct-response and classified money inside it. Grade C: proxy-derived in full. || AGGREGATION: plain median of three lens centrals (structural-proxy 36.75, reference-class 38.34, Fermi-decomposition 38.92). No extremizing (rule 1): the lenses share the Coen table, the MAGNA column and the same source hunt. No lens discounted. ROUTE CONSOLIDATION APPLIED BEFORE ANY WEIGHTING. The panel presented about fourteen named routes across three lenses; they collapse to eight independent evidence bases, because routes sharing a common input are one route. The Coen national/local geography residual was offered seven times, MAGNA via Statistical Abstract T1279 six times, the 1997 Economic Census three times, DMA/WEFA three times with three different discount factors, the Knight Ridder 10-K three times, and the IAB format and pricing shares five times. CONSEQUENCE FOR THIS POOL: there are exactly TWO independent evidence bases (Coen geography, MAGNA) plus one one-year, one-medium official check. The apparent three-route corroboration is one route wearing three hats, which is why the interval stays wide. || E1 Coen national/local geography residual, WEIGHT 0.60. PROXY-POPULATION GAP: the proxy population is 'money bought by a national buyer', the target population is 'money bought on brand terms'; the gap is direct mail, directories, general-media direct response and non-newspaper classified sitting inside the National geography. ADJUSTMENT: carve all four out; the unadjusted bias runs UP, size about 3.5pp. || E2 MAGNA Direct/National/Local, Statistical Abstract Table 1279, WEIGHT 0.25. PROXY-POPULATION GAP: supplier revenue on a $177.5bn universe against advertiser billings on $247.5bn (-28.3 percent); MAGNA carries no equivalent of Coen's $32.1bn miscellaneous bucket ($24.4bn of it national) and no business papers; and its National/Local boundary is SELLER-side while Coen's is BUYER-side, putting roughly $8.7bn of national spot TV and radio on the other side. ADJUSTMENT: transfer STRUCTURE, not levels, and strip miscellaneous from both sides, which brings the construction to 30.89 percent against MAGNA's published 30.14 percent - a 0.75pp agreement, and the load-bearing corroboration for the whole geographic spine. || E3 1997 Economic Census NAICS 5131 Sources of Receipts (grade A), WEIGHT 0.10. PROXY-POPULATION GAP: receipts are NET of agency commission, which is levied on national money and largely not on local direct sales; the census excludes cable networks, which are overwhelmingly national; and it is 1997 not 2000, broadcast only. ADJUSTMENT: gross national up at an 11 percent realised commission rate (43.8 to 47.2 percent), then add cable at roughly 76 percent national (to about 52.6 percent); residual gap to Coen's implied 55.7 percent is about 3pp. This validates the geography spine, NOT the money-type reassignment. || E4 DMA/WEFA, WEIGHT 0.05, entering only as the general-media direct-response block carved OUT of this pool. || INTERVAL: min lower to max upper across the lenses. Its 11.5pp width is honest - 4.9pp is the unresolved Coen-versus-MAGNA basis gap, about 3pp the unpublished composition of Coen's miscellaneous bucket, 1.5pp the general-media direct-response allowance, and 0.9pp Coen's own restatement of Total National for 2000 between its 2001 and curated vintages.

claims.statement: Local-retail advertising was 28.3 percent of the $247.5B US measured advertising market in 2000, about $70.1B: local newspaper retail display, local spot TV, local radio, local cable, local out-of-home and local miscellaneous, after removing newspaper classified, the classified inside shoppers and weeklies, and the local share of general-media direct response. claims.unit: percent of total US ad spend
claims.method: SOURCED BY: no source. No compiler published a local-RETAIL pool, only a Local GEOGRAPHY containing classified and directory money. Grade C. || AGGREGATION: plain median of three lens centrals (structural-proxy 23.005, reference-class 28.32, Fermi-decomposition 29.61). No extremizing. ROUTE CONSOLIDATION APPLIED BEFORE ANY WEIGHTING. The panel presented about fourteen named routes across three lenses; they collapse to eight independent evidence bases, because routes sharing a common input are one route. The Coen national/local geography residual was offered seven times, MAGNA via Statistical Abstract T1279 six times, the 1997 Economic Census three times, DMA/WEFA three times with three different discount factors, the Knight Ridder 10-K three times, and the IAB format and pricing shares five times. || E1 Coen Total Local residual, WEIGHT 0.60. PROXY-POPULATION GAP: the same geography-for-money-type substitution as national brand, mirrored. ADJUSTMENT: subtract NAA newspaper classified $19,608m, the shopper and weekly classified fringe, and the local share of general-media direct response. CONTAINMENT VERIFIED, not assumed: NAA retail $21,409m + NAA classified $19,608m = $41,017m sits inside Coen's local newspaper line of $41,821m with $804m to spare, checked for all eight years, so the classified carve-out never overdraws the line. || E3 1997 Economic Census local receipts (grade A), WEIGHT 0.15. Gap and adjustment as for national brand, applied in the opposite direction: after commission-grossing and cable exclusion the census implies a local broadcast share near 47-48 percent against Coen's structural 44-47 percent - a 1-3pp agreement on one medium group in one year. || E7 and E8, the shopper, weekly and trade classified fringe removed from this pool, WEIGHT 0.10 combined. Two genuinely independent builds: supply-side (decompose Coen's $7,665m local miscellaneous into weeklies, shoppers, local point-of-purchase and transit, then apply classified intensity by publication type) and demand-side (households x classified placement rate x price, plus non-employer firms and local service providers). They share no input and land at $1.85-1.9bn and $1.7bn, a 12 percent agreement - the only place in the panel where two independent routes converge on an unsourced quantity. || E4 DMA/WEFA local share of general-media direct response, WEIGHT 0.05. || E2 MAGNA Local, WEIGHT 0.10, INTERVAL ONLY. Explicitly tested and REJECTED as a level check by two lenses, and the rejection is itself a finding: MAGNA's Local is 51.2 percent of its universe against Coen's 38.7 percent, but MAGNA local radio $18,819m less Coen local radio $14,847m is almost exactly Coen's national spot radio $3,668m, so the gap is the seller-side versus buyer-side boundary, not a disagreement about money. A money-type axis is about the buyer, so Coen's treatment is correct here and MAGNA sets the ceiling only. || INTERVAL: min lower to max upper across the lenses. The 12.2pp width is dominated by one definitional question, not by measurement error: 4.50pp of the downside is the directory convention alone (whether local Yellow Pages, $11,135m in 2000, belongs in this pool at all). See open_taxonomy_questions in reconciled.json.

claims.method: SOURCED BY: PARTIAL AND DOMINANT. NAA newspaper classified (grade B, all eight years, already in adspend.json as series.naa_newspaper) is $19,608m for 2000 = 89.5 percent of this pool's central, and it is used AS PUBLISHED: a proposed rebasing onto Coen's slightly larger newspaper line (+$153m) is NOT applied, because it is a construction and the source is not. It is corroborated independently at grade A by Knight Ridder's audited FY2000 10-K. THE POOL still grades C, and the reason is precise: the remaining 10.5 percent is unsourced construction, and it is the construction that makes this a pool rather than a newspaper figure. The sourced sub-object is separately recorded at grade B - newspaper classified was 7.923 percent of the observed US total in 2000, with the SHARE peak in 1997 at 8.944 percent (path: 1994 8.145, 1995 8.434, 1996 8.597, 1997 8.944, 1998 8.647, 1999 8.389, 2000 7.923, 2001 7.187), numerator and denominator both published, nothing derived. || AGGREGATION: plain median of three lens centrals (structural-proxy 8.63, reference-class 8.85, Fermi-decomposition 9.142) - the tightest agreement in the era, because 89.5 percent of the pool is a real published series. || SOURCE LEG, WEIGHT 0.87: the NAA published series, used as published. || E5 Knight Ridder FY2000 10-K, corroboration only, no weight on the central. PROXY-POPULATION GAP: listed newspaper groups are metro-skewed and metro dailies carry a higher classified share than the small-daily tail of NAA's universe, so the filings figure of 42.5 percent is an UPPER bound on the industry ratio. The 2.2pp gap against NAA's 40.3 percent is in exactly the expected direction and at the expected size. Summing the roughly fifteen public groups' 10-Ks would lift this spine from B to A. || E7 supply-side fringe build, WEIGHT 0.05. PROXY-POPULATION GAP: Coen has never published the composition of its $32,083m miscellaneous bucket, and shoppers and weeklies are demonstrably not inside Coen's newspaper line (Coen $49,050m against NAA $48,670m leaves no room). ADJUSTMENT: bottom-up from roughly 4,000-5,000 free and shopper titles plus 7,000 paid weeklies, capped top-down at half of Coen's $7,665m local miscellaneous, with classified intensity applied separately by publication type (about 45 percent for shoppers, 12-25 percent for paid weeklies, 5-8 percent for trade press) because a shopper IS a classified vehicle while a paid weekly resembles a small daily. || E8 demand-side buyer-count build, WEIGHT 0.05, genuinely independent of E7 and agreeing within 12 percent. || E6 IAB/PwC classifieds share applied to Coen's internet line, WEIGHT 0.03. PROXY-POPULATION GAP: two offsetting definitional biases - IAB's classifieds category absorbs auction listing revenue (overstates) but misses classified sold inside newspaper print-plus-online bundles and, far more importantly, the pure-play job, auto and property portals that sold direct with no agency in the loop (understates). ARITHMETIC DEFECT CORRECTED: the superseded method took 7 percent of IAB's $8,225m total ($576m) against a Coen grand total carrying only $6,507m of internet; on the Coen line the same share is $455m, so the old method imported $121m that was not in the denominator. || INTERVAL: min lower to max upper across the lenses, 2.2pp - the narrowest in the era.

claims.statement: Direct-response advertising was 24.7 percent of the $247.5B US measured advertising market in 2000, about $61.2B: direct mail $44.6B, national directories $2.1B, performance-priced internet $0.7-1.4B and direct-response money bought inside general media $5-18.5B. That is 5.5 points above the floor the record carried before, and every lens moved it up.
claims.unit: percent of total US ad spend
claims.method: SOURCED BY: PARTIAL, at component level only. Direct mail $44,591m is Coen's own published line (grade B) and is 73 percent of this pool's central. No source publishes this POOL on this denominator. Two compilers publish incompatible direct-response objects and BOTH are LARGER than the superseded construction: MAGNA's 'Direct' domain (grade A, free for 2000 via Statistical Abstract Table 1279) at $31,108m on a $177.5bn supplier-revenue universe, and DMA/WEFA (grade B) at $191.6bn on a $339.3bn universe that counts $73.2bn of telemarketing. Neither is commensurable with the Coen denominator, so neither wins outright; both constrain the interval and both raise the floor. Grade C. || AGGREGATION: plain median of three lens centrals (structural-proxy 22.62, reference-class 24.71, Fermi-decomposition 31.102). The spread is the widest in the era and is driven by two disclosed convention choices, not by conflicting evidence. ROUTE CONSOLIDATION APPLIED BEFORE ANY WEIGHTING. The panel presented about fourteen named routes across three lenses; they collapse to eight independent evidence bases, because routes sharing a common input are one route. The Coen national/local geography residual was offered seven times, MAGNA via Statistical Abstract T1279 six times, the 1997 Economic Census three times, DMA/WEFA three times with three different discount factors, the Knight Ridder 10-K three times, and the IAB format and pricing shares five times. || E1 Coen's own direct mail and Yellow Pages lines, WEIGHT 0.45. Direct mail alone is 18.02pp of the 24.71pp central. PROXY-POPULATION GAP: none for the medium, but a basis gap that is stated rather than adjusted - Coen books direct mail at full advertiser program cost while every other Coen medium is space only. || E2 MAGNA 'Direct' domain, WEIGHT 0.15. PROXY-POPULATION GAP: MAGNA's direct mail is carriage-only supplier revenue at $18,250m against Coen's $44,591m full advertiser outlay, a documented 2.44x. ADJUSTMENT: substitute Coen's direct-mail line into MAGNA's own classification and gross the denominator by the same amount, giving $57,449m / $203,841m = 28.2 percent - and MAGNA's Direct excludes direct-response TV, print and radio and telemarketing by its own construction, so 28.2 percent is a FLOOR from an independent compiler's own structure. Two lenses derived this separately. || E4 DMA/WEFA direct-marketing-by-medium, WEIGHT 0.20, CEILING-SETTING. PROXY-POPULATION GAP, and it is large: DMA measures response-CARRYING placements and includes traffic generation (drive-to-store with a call to action), not response-BOUGHT money; it counts telemarketing as advertising; its newspaper direct-response share of 37.3 percent ($18.4bn) almost exactly reproduces NAA's classified ($19.6bn), so it double-counts against the classified pool; and its direct-mail line matches Coen to $9m, proving it is NOT independent on the very medium it appears to corroborate. ADJUSTMENT: applied raw it yields $104.2bn of general-media direct response and a 48.9 percent pool, which all three lenses reject; the discounts applied ranged from a 3x medium-by-medium discount (to $18.5bn) through a roughly 75 percent discount (to $7.9bn) to a bottom-up rebuild (about $5.0bn). || E10 and E11, the ERA/infomercial direct-response-TV build and the PIB 1993 magazine mail-order category, WEIGHT 0.15 combined. These are the ONLY genuinely independent checks on the general-media direct-response quantity, and both land at the bottom of the range: ERA's $11bn of US direct-TV sales less $8.5bn of shopping-channel owned airtime that is outside measured advertising implies $3.5-5.3bn of direct-response television against DMA's $21.9bn, and PIB's magazine mail-order category was 9.8 percent of Coen magazines in 1993 against DMA's 56.6 percent. || E6 IAB/PwC pricing-model split, WEIGHT 0.05. PROXY-POPULATION GAP: IAB's denominator ($8,087-8,225m) exceeds Coen's internet line ($6,507m), so the share must be applied to Coen's line or money absent from the denominator is imported. ARITHMETIC DEFECT CORRECTED: the superseded method took 10 percent of IAB's $8,225m ($822m) against a denominator carrying $6,507m of internet; on the Coen line it is $651m, so the old method imported $172m. || E9 USPS Standard Mail (A) postage revenue, WEIGHT 0.0 on the central but named because it ADJUDICATES the basis: at roughly $15-16bn in FY2000 it puts Coen at 2.8-3.0x postage (postage plus production, creative and list rental, i.e. total advertiser outlay) and MAGNA at 1.15x (media-owner revenue plus a thin margin). Since a money-type split asks where ADVERTISER money goes, Coen's basis is the correct one for this partition. This route narrows the interval rather than widening it. || STATEMENT DEFECT CORRECTED: the superseded method said direct-response television and print insertions 'are not separable in the Coen series'. Not separable in COEN is true; not separable is false - DMA/WEFA published them by medium for 2000 (DR-television $21.9bn, DR-newspaper $18.4bn, DR-magazine $9.8bn, DR-radio $7.7bn). They need heavy discounting but they are not zero. || INTERVAL: min lower to max upper across the lenses, 17.0pp - the widest in the era, and correctly so.

claims.statement: On the cross-era comparable rule, where ALL directory money sits in the same intent pool eras 6 and 7 use, local-retail advertising was 23.8 percent of the $247.5B US measured advertising market in 2000, about $58.9B. That is the era-native pool (e5-scale-011, 28.3 percent) less local Yellow Pages, $11,135m or 4.50 points of the market. Under the era-native geographic rule local retail leads direct response, 28.32 to 24.71; under this unified-intent rule direct response leads local retail, 29.21 to 23.82. The flip is exact and this one block is its sole cause. Under BOTH rules the two intervals still overlap, so the pair stays unranked by interval and a chart must not sort these two bars. No 1994-2001 evidence decides which rule is right; both are carried.
claims.unit: percent of total US ad spend
claims.method: TAXONOMY: unified-intent. This is the CROSS-ERA COMPARABLE view of era 5's local-retail pool, and it is a declared definitional seam, not a correction. The era-native claim (e5-scale-011 / e5-buyers-011) stands unchanged at 28.32 percent and is the view era 5 reports on its own terms. || THE BLOCK THAT MOVES: local Yellow Pages, $11,135m in 2000, which is 4.4995 percent of the observed $247,472m Coen total. The national directory leg, $2,093m, already sits in direct response under both rules, so only the local leg moves. Both legs are Coen's own published Yellow Pages line for 2000 ($13,228m) split by advertiser geography. || DERIVATION: this claim inherits the era-native pool's whole evidence base, three-lens panel and aggregation rule, and changes exactly one convention. Central = 28.32 - 4.4995 = 23.82 percent, $70,084m - $11,135m = $58,949m. Every other input is untouched: the Coen Total Local residual (E1, weight 0.60), the 1997 Economic Census local receipts check (E3, weight 0.15), the supply-side and demand-side shopper-and-weekly classified fringe builds (E7/E8, weight 0.10 combined, independent of each other and agreeing within 12 percent), the DMA/WEFA local share of general-media direct response (E4, weight 0.05) and MAGNA Local as a ceiling only (E2, weight 0.10, interval only). The containment check still holds and was not re-run because it does not touch directories: NAA retail $21,409m + NAA classified $19,608m = $41,017m sits inside Coen's local newspaper line of $41,821m with $804m to spare, verified for all eight years. || INTERVAL, and it NARROWS rather than shifting whole. Native ci80 [20.8, 33.0], 12.2pp wide. UPPER BOUND: 33.0 - 4.4995 = 28.50. The native ceiling was set by the reference-class and Fermi lenses, both of which carried the local directory block inside this pool, so removing the block lowers the ceiling by the whole block. LOWER BOUND: unchanged at 20.8. The reconciliation attributes 4.50pp of the native 7.52pp downside to the directory convention alone; under this rule that convention is settled by construction, so what is left below the central is the 3.02pp of measurement and construction dispersion the lenses actually disagree about, and 23.82 - 3.02 = 20.80. claims.statement: The four reconciled money-type pools sum to 100.22 percent of the observed $247.5B US total for 2000, over-allocating it by $544 million. The over-allocation is an artefact of taking a median pool by pool: each lens's own partition closes exactly, but the median of a partition is not itself a partition. It is reported rather than smoothed away.
claims.unit: percentage points of the observed 2000 US total; negative means the four pools over-allocate
claims.method: The four pool medians sum to 100.22 percent of the observed 2000 total, over-allocating the $247,472m observed total by $544m. This is not a measurement gap and not a shortfall: it is an exact, fully attributable artefact of the median operator. Each of the three lenses individually reconciles to 100.000 percent by construction, but the median of a partition is not itself a partition. The over-allocation traces to a single swap: the medians for national brand (38.34), local retail (28.32) and direct response (24.71) all come from the Fermi-decomposition lens, whose own four values sum to 100.00 with classified at 8.63; the classified median is 8.85, from the reference-class lens, and 8.85 - 8.63 = 0.22 exactly. BOUNDS: taking the mean of lens centrals instead of the median reconciles to 100.000 exactly, and dropping any one lens and taking the mean of the remaining two also reconciles to within 0.003pp, so the residual cannot exceed roughly half a point under any plausible re-specification of the aggregation rule. It is left standing rather than smoothed away, because scaling the four pools by 0.9978 would silently move each headline off the plain median the rigor standard requires. || SECOND, LARGER RESIDUAL, WHICH NO FORCING CAN ABSORB. The in-universe residual above is trivial, but the observed Coen universe excludes money that functionally belongs in these pools. (a) TELEMARKETING: DMA counts $73.2bn of it as advertising in 2000; Coen counts none. That is 29.6 percent of the observed total, and if it were in the denominator direct response would dominate every other pool. This is a scope choice, not a measurement error, and it is the single largest definitional question in the era. (b) ONLINE LISTING AND POSTING REVENUE: Forrester put the whole US online recruitment market at $1.2bn in 2000, more than double IAB's ENTIRE classifieds format ($566m), and a bottom-up build from named sellers puts real online classified near $1.0bn against the $455m that fits inside Coen's internet line. Job-posting and resume-database fees were never counted as advertising by anyone, so roughly $0.5-1.0bn of what was functionally classified money - about half the online classified pool at the moment of the migration - sits outside every series here. Two lenses found this independently. (c) 1994 HAS NO DIRECT-RESPONSE SOURCE OF ANY KIND: the WEFA series begins in 1995 and 1994 is backcast at the published 1995-2000 medium-weighted CAGR of 8.69 percent, so that year's direct-response figure should render as a visible hole, not as a point.

open_defect.status: OPEN - NOT REPAIRED. No value in this claim has been changed.
open_defect.where: The secondary share in this claim's statement, and the identical phrase in the parent event's desc field.
open_defect.problem: 'close to 20% of the 61 spots available' cannot be true against the counts stated in the same sentence. 21/61 = 34.4 percent; the narrower count 14/61 = 23.0 percent; and 20 percent of 61 = 12.2 ads, which matches neither 14 nor 21. Everything else in the sentence reconciles: 14 + 5 + 2 = 21, and $44M / 21 = $2.10M per spot against the stated ~$2.2M.
open_defect.unaffected: central 14, ci80 [14, 21], unit, grade B and as_of 2000-01-30 are not in question. The defect is a percentage carried in prose, not the calibrated value.
open_defect.why_not_repaired: The sweep did not establish the correct figure from a source. Two readings are open - a corrupted 'close to 20 OF the 61 spots' (21 is close to 20), or the true share of about a third - and 34 percent and 20 percent tell materially different stories about how far the bubble reached into the Super Bowl. Writing either without re-reading the Wikipedia and Fast Company sources would be inventing a replacement number, which this repair does not do.
open_defect.resolution_required: Human decision, or a fresh source read of the two cited sources, before this sentence is quoted anywhere.
open_defect.chapter_exposure: None. Chapter 06 (06-the-impression.md) carries only the fourteen in-game advertisers and the ~$2.2M spot price, neither of which is affected.
open_defect.source_carries_the_error: The figure is NOT a paraphrase error introduced by this project: the R3 verdict on this claim quotes the cited Wikipedia article as saying the 21 ads 'amounted to nearly 20% of the 61 spots available', and R3 imported that string verbatim. The impossibility therefore sits in the source, so repairing it means deciding whether to correct the source's arithmetic (about a third), read it as a corrupted 'nearly 20 OF the 61 spots', or drop the share entirely. That is a human call on the source, not a data-entry fix.

claims.method: Numerator: impression-priced US internet ad revenue in 2000 = banners (48%) plus sponsorships (28%) of IAB/PwC FY2000 revenue $8.225B = $6.25B. Denominator: US delivered display impressions in 2000, triangulated three ways. (1) AdRelevance measured 172 billion US impressions in Q4 2000 and 65 billion in December 2000; with Q4 the seasonal peak at roughly 28-30% of the year, that implies 575-615 billion for 2000, and AdRelevance's monitoring method undercounts unmeasured sites, so treat it as a floor. (2) DoubleClick's DART served 621 billion ads worldwide in 2000 for 2,000+ clients; DART was the largest but far from the only ad server (Yahoo, AOL and MSN ran their own; AdForce, Engage and 24/7 competed), so if DART was 25-40% of worldwide served ads the worldwide total was 1.6-2.5 trillion and the US share roughly half of that. (3) Yahoo alone delivered about 784 million page views per day ex-Japan in December 2000, roughly 24 billion in the month. Taking the three together, US delivered display impressions in 2000 were between 0.6 and 1.5 trillion, central 0.9 trillion. $6.25B / 0.9T = $0.0069 per impression. Cross-check: Yahoo's marketing-services revenue of $968.3M over an estimated 222 billion ex-Japan page views for 2000 (linear interpolation between 431M/day ex-Japan in December 1999 and 784M/day ex-Japan in December 2000) gives $4.37 per thousand page views, in the same band. CI reflects the impression-count uncertainty, which dominates.

claims.statement: Direct cost of serving one web ad impression in 2000 — roughly $0.90 per thousand at portal scale, comprising content, bandwidth and equipment depreciation (about $0.68 per thousand page views at Yahoo) plus ad-delivery infrastructure (about $0.09 per thousand ads at DoubleClick). Marginal cost was trivially small; the era's real cost was the human ad sales force, which Yahoo carried at 38% of revenue.
claims.unit: USD per delivered ad impression
claims.method: Two audited anchors, summed. (a) Ad-delivery infrastructure: DoubleClick TechSolutions FY2000 revenue $203.4M at 71.6% gross margin implies cost of ad delivery (internet access, ad-delivery system depreciation, facilities, operating personnel) of $57.8M against 621 billion ads served = $0.000093 per ad, i.e. $0.093 per thousand. (b) Publisher content and bandwidth: Yahoo FY2000 cost of revenues $149.744M (third-party content fees, internet connection charges, equipment depreciation, production) against an estimated 222 billion ex-Japan page views for 2000 (linear interpolation between 431M/day ex-Japan in December 1999 and 784M/day ex-Japan in December 2000) = $0.675 per thousand page views. Sum at portal scale ~$0.77 per thousand impressions; central raised to $0.90 because smaller publishers ran materially worse infrastructure economics than Yahoo. CI upper bound of $2.50 per thousand covers content-heavy publishers; lower bound covers pure-network sellers with no content cost.
